segments.text: Snakes for hair. A gaze that turns people to stone. Medusa is one of the most famous monsters of Greek myth. Today, she is also seen as a victim, a woman punished for something that was done to her. So which is she? The answer depends on which source you read.

In this episode, we follow Medusa across seven centuries of Greek and Roman poetry and art: an early poem about the gods, faces on ancient shields and temples, a painted vase at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a Roman poet who told her story in a new way.

One of the earliest accounts comes from the Greek poet Hesiod, around 700 BCE. In his Theogony, a poem about the origins of the gods, Medusa is one of three Gorgon sisters, daughters of ancient sea deities. Her sisters, Stheno and Euryale, are immortal. Medusa alone is mortal.

Hesiod tells us very little about her. He says that Poseidon lay with her in a soft meadow among spring flowers, and that when Perseus cut off her head, the winged horse Pegasus and Chrysaor, named for his golden sword, sprang from her. There is no curse and no punishment. In Hesiod, Medusa is simply born a Gorgon.

Early Greek artists gave the Gorgon an unforgettable face. In the sixth century BCE, she often looks like this: wide, staring eyes, a grinning mouth, sharp tusks, and a protruding tongue. She is not meant to be beautiful. She is meant to be seen.

Faces like this, called gorgoneia, appeared on shields, on drinking cups, and on the tiles along temple roofs. Many scholars think they were meant to frighten away harm. The monster's face could also serve as a guardian.

Even the goddess Athena carried it. As early as Homer's Iliad, the Gorgon's head appears on the aegis, Athena's protective goatskin. The face of the defeated monster became part of the goddess's own power.

Over time, the image began to change. Around 490 BCE, the poet Pindar spoke of fair-cheeked Medusa. He also told how Athena invented a melody for the aulos, a reed pipe, to imitate the lament of the Gorgons for their sister.

On this vase at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, painted in Athens around 450 BCE, Perseus comes upon Medusa as she sleeps, with Athena close by. Medusa still has wings, but her face is young and calm. The museum describes it as one of the earliest images of Medusa with an attractive face.

Why did artists begin to show her this way? Scholars have suggested several reasons, from changing ideals of beauty to new ways of telling the story. The sources do not give a single answer. But by the fifth century BCE, Medusa could be both terrifying and beautiful.

The version best known today comes later, from Rome. Around the year 8 CE, the poet Ovid completed his Metamorphoses, a long poem about transformations. In Book Four, Perseus himself tells the story. Medusa, he says, was once a beautiful young woman, admired above all for her hair.

Then, it is said, Neptune, the Roman name for Poseidon, assaulted her in the temple of Minerva, the Roman Athena. The goddess hid her face behind her aegis. And so that the act would not go unpunished, she changed Medusa's hair into snakes.

Ovid wrote about seven hundred years after Hesiod, and he often reshaped older myths in his own way. Other ancient writers give other reasons. The mythographer known as Apollodorus reports a version in which Medusa wished to rival Athena in beauty.

Medusa's story lived on long after the ancient world. In the early 1800s, the sculptor Antonio Canova carved Perseus holding up her head in triumph. For Medusa's face, Canova followed an ancient marble mask of a beautiful, sorrowful Medusa. The hero is the center of this statue.

In the twentieth century, many writers and artists returned to Ovid's version and read Medusa as a woman who was wronged, and then blamed. That reading is a modern interpretation. But it is built on an ancient text.

So is Medusa a monster or a victim? In Hesiod, she is born a Gorgon. On early temples and shields, her face protects. On a classical vase, she sleeps with a young, calm face. And in Ovid, she is a woman punished for what was done to her.
There is no single original Medusa. Each source shows how a different time imagined her. Every story has an origin. Medusa has many.
